name: Hartshorn

lead: Hartshorn originally meant the antler of male red deer. Distilling antler produced oil of hartshorn, and from it salt of hartshorn (ammonium carbonate) and spirit of hartshorn (aqueous ammonia).

Old beauty recipes included it, sometimes as ground calcined antler used as a pale powder, in face washes meant to give a fairer-looking complexion. It also served as smelling salts and a baking leavener.

paras: Historical sources describe calcined hartshorn ground to powder and dissolved with other ingredients in rosewater for washing the face, and salt of hartshorn used as a sweating agent and revival salt. Modern use is mostly as a baking leavener.

Ammonia vapour irritates the eyes, nose and lungs, and strong ammonia solutions can burn skin. Nineteenth-century health journals carried articles on hartshorn dangers, and baking with it can form acrylamide.

web.title: An excellent cosmetic for the face

chain: Calcined antler or salt is mixed into a face wash
A paler, smoother-looking complexion, as historical recipes intended
angle.text: In historical beauty recipes hartshorn was an ingredient in washes meant to lighten and smooth the face. Practitioners today are more likely to meet it as smelling salts or baking ammonia.

lead: Hartshorn is the antler of male red deer, and by extension the nitrogen compounds historically distilled from it. Oil of hartshorn was a crude distillate, salt of hartshorn is ammonium carbonate, and spirit of hartshorn is an archaic name for aqueous ammonia.[1]

Its appearance-related use is historical. An eighteenth-century complexion wash recipe, attributed to The Toilet of Flora or Abdeker, calls for a pound of levigated hartshorn dissolved with other ingredients in rose-water for washing the face. A blogger who tested the recipe suggested the ingredient was probably ground calcined antler used as a white pigment rather than ammonia salt.[2]
Other documented uses are medicinal, as a sweating agent for fevers, smelling salts, and a leavening agent in older European baking.[1] No clinical studies on hartshorn for skin exist.

paras: Oil of hartshorn is a crude product of destructive distillation of antler; salt of hartshorn is made by dry distillation of that oil.[1] Calcinated or charred hartshorn was used as an absorbent.[1]

Hartshorn jelly and decoctions were used for diarrhea, and the salt was a sudorific for fevers; it was also applied for insect bites, stings and sunstroke.[1] Nineteenth-century popular journals discussed ammonia, or hartshorn, and its dangers.[3][4]
The complexion wash recipe in Toilet of Flora-era literature uses hartshorn alongside rice powder and ceruse in rose-water.[2]
Ammonia is an irritant. Baking with ammonium salts can produce acrylamide, which the Wikipedia article describes as a carcinogen.[1]
